253.title: You haven't been there (Avot 2:4)
253.hook: Hillel: don't separate from the community; don't judge until you've stood in their place
253.howItsDone: Hillel's warning is studied alongside the teaching to judge every person favorably, as a daily habit of thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabban Gamaliel's mirror, ratzon: do God's will as your own. Your line was want what's good. Today, Hillel is back.

The woman in the checkout line snaps at her kid, and everyone around her silently decides what kind of mother she is. The coworker who's been late three times this month. The neighbor who never mows his lawn. These verdicts arrive in an instant, and they feel very sure. What nobody sees is the hospital visit that morning, or the second job, or the thing nobody talks about at home. Hillel, the gentle sage from the roof in the snow, has five short warnings in chapter two. The middle one is about exactly this.
screen: `THE MOTHER IN THE CHECKOUT LINE.` → `AN INSTANT, VERY SURE.` → `WHAT WE DON'T SEE.`

segments.voice: Here they are. Don't separate yourself from the community. Don't be sure of yourself until the day you die. Don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place. Don't say something that can't be understood, hoping it'll be understood later. And don't say, when I have free time I'll study, because maybe you won't. Look at the middle one. Makom in Hebrew: his place, his spot, where he's standing. Not until you've heard about it. Until you've gotten there. Now the line right before it: don't be sure of yourself until the day you die. The Talmud tells of a high priest who served faithfully for eighty years, and then, at the very end, left the path of the sages. Nobody is beyond slipping. Put the two lines side by side: you can't be too sure about yourself, and you can't be too sure about the other person. You don't know how you'd act in their place, because you've never stood there. Some teachers point out something quietly radical in the wording. Can you ever really reach another person's place? Their childhood, their body, their worst morning? Maybe never completely. Which would mean the judgment always waits. That doesn't mean anything goes; Jewish law has courts and judges. But in everyday life, Hillel asks for a pause, and a little humility, before the verdict.
screen: `HILLEL'S FIVE WARNINGS.` · `UNTIL YOU'VE REACHED HIS PLACE.` · `DON'T BE SURE OF YOURSELF.` · `CAN YOU EVER REACH IT?` · then, large: `YOU HAVEN'T BEEN THERE.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've judged lately, and don't argue about whether you were right. Imagine waking up in their bed this morning: their worries, their body, their bank account, the conversation they're dreading. Walk slowly through their morning until the moment you judged, and notice if anything shifts.
Makom. His place, where he stands: the word in Hillel's warning not to judge your fellow until you've reached it.
Your line: nobody is beyond slipping. Not them, and not you either. That's day two hundred fifty-three.

254.title: Be a mensch (Avot 2:5)
254.hook: Hillel: where there are no decent people, strive to be one
254.howItsDone: Calling someone a mensch is a common Jewish compliment for integrity and kindness, and parents and teachers often quote Hillel's line when urging children to do the decent thing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel said don't judge anyone until you've reached their place. Your line was nobody is beyond slipping.

A man drops a bag of groceries on a busy sidewalk. Oranges roll everywhere. Twenty people see it. They slow down, look, and keep walking, because surely somebody else will help. Then one person stops, crouches down, and starts picking up oranges. Suddenly two more people stop too. If you've spent any time around Jewish grandparents, you have a word for that first person: mensch. And the idea goes back to one line of Hillel.
screen: `ORANGES ON THE SIDEWALK.` → `TWENTY PEOPLE KEEP WALKING.` → `ONE PERSON STOPS.`

segments.voice: Mensch is Yiddish, from the German word for a human being. In Yiddish it grew into something more: a person of integrity, decent, kind and trustworthy, someone who does the right thing without being asked. Calling someone a real mensch is one of the highest compliments there is, and it has nothing to do with money, fame or cleverness. In Pirkei Avot, Hillel gives a short list of who can and can't do what. A person who's too bashful can't learn, because they won't ask questions. A person who's short-tempered can't teach. Then his final line: in a place where there are no people, try to be a person. The Hebrew for person there is ish, and it clearly means more than just being human. It means someone who stands up. When nobody is stepping forward, you step forward. When nobody is being decent, you be the decent one. Commentators read it a couple of ways. The plain way: when no one else is taking responsibility, take it. Another: even where there's no one around to see you, still act like a real person. Either way, Hillel's word is strive. Try hard. It isn't easy to be the first one to stop on the sidewalk; everyone else walking on pulls on you. Being a mensch means feeling that pull and crouching down anyway. And once one person does, others often follow.

segments.voice: Think of a place you'll be today, a meeting, a family chat, a train, a classroom, where something goes undone because everyone waits for someone else: the dishes after dinner, the new person nobody talks to, the joke that goes too far. Picture yourself being the one who moves first, just once, and feel what that's like.
Mensch. Yiddish for a human being, and for a decent one. Hillel said: in a place where there are no people, strive to be a person.
Your line: crouch down anyway. Ish, mensch: a person in the full sense. Two hundred fifty-four days in.

255.title: The skull on the water (Avot 2:6)
255.hook: Hillel sees a skull floating and says: because you drowned others, you were drowned
255.howItsDone: Jewish teaching speaks of 'measure for measure' (middah keneged middah) as a pattern in how the world works, while leaving judgment to God and the courts rather than to private revenge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, oranges on the sidewalk and Hillel's line: where there are no people, strive to be a person. Your line was crouch down anyway.

Hillel is at the water's edge. Something is floating on the surface, turning slowly in the current. He looks closer. It's a human skull. He doesn't scream, and he doesn't walk away. He speaks to it: only a handful of words, in Aramaic, the everyday language of his time. Pirkei Avot is mostly sayings, short, wise, a little abstract. And right in the middle of chapter two sits this scene out of a ghost story.
screen: `SOMETHING ON THE WATER.` → `HILLEL SPEAKS TO IT.` → `A SCENE, NOT A SAYING.`

segments.voice: Here's what he says. Because you drowned others, they drowned you. And in the end, the ones who drowned you will be drowned. That's the whole thing. The Mishnah doesn't say whose skull it was, or where, or when, or how Hillel knew. Only the words. The first half sounds like simple payback: you did it, so it was done to you. The rabbis have a name for this idea, measure for measure: what a person sends out tends to come back in kind. But the second half is where the saying turns. The ones who drowned you will be drowned too. The people who killed this man aren't heroes of justice. They've just joined the cycle, and it doesn't stop with them. Violence answered by violence doesn't end anything; it hands the drowning on to the next person. Commentators are careful here. This isn't a claim that everyone who suffers must have deserved it. Hillel is speaking to one skull, not about every victim in the world. Some commentators read it as a statement about God's justice, which works in ways people can't see and don't get to take into their own hands. So it's a warning in two directions. Don't be the one who drowns others. And don't appoint yourself to drown the drowner. Harm comes back. The only way out of the circle is for someone to stop pushing.
screen: `A SKULL, AND A FEW WORDS.` · `MEASURE FOR MEASURE.` · `THE DROWNERS WILL BE DROWNED.` · `SOMEONE HAS TO STOP PUSHING.` · then, large: `HARM COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of a small circle of hurt going back and forth in your life, nothing dramatic: a sibling who snipes and you snipe back, a coworker you both undercut, a comment section. Imagine the next turn is yours, and you simply don't take it, no reply in kind. Picture the circle slowing down.
Hillel, who spoke to a skull floating on the water: because you drowned others, they drowned you, and so will those who drowned you.
Your line: harm comes back. Measure for measure, unless someone stops pushing. See you tomorrow.

256.title: More isn't more (Avot 2:7)
256.hook: more flesh, more worms; more possessions, more worry; more Torah, more life
256.howItsDone: Giving tzedakah, charity understood as justice, is a central Jewish practice, and some households keep a tzedakah box and drop coins in before Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel spoke to a skull on the water and warned about the circle of revenge. Your line was harm comes back.

The shoes, the gadget, the bigger apartment: the thing someone really wanted, finally bought. For a few days, it was wonderful. Then, quietly, it came with things. A password to remember. A warranty to register. A thing to insure, to clean, to worry about scratching. A rented storage unit is a monument to this feeling. Hillel noticed it too, and turned it into a saying with a beat. It sounds almost like a chant.
screen: `THE THING YOU REALLY WANTED.` → `IT CAME WITH THINGS.` → `A SAYING LIKE A CHANT.`

segments.voice: Here's how his list begins. More flesh, more worms. More possessions, more worry. It's blunt. A body fattened on luxury ends in the same grave as everyone else's, and the more you own, the more you have to guard. In Hebrew it has a beat: marbeh nekhasim, marbeh de'agah. The list goes on through the households of his ancient world, with a few lines about servants and wives that read uncomfortably today, and are honestly part of the text. Then the list turns. More Torah, more life. More sitting in study, more wisdom. More counsel, more understanding. More tzedakah, giving to those in need, more peace. Hillel isn't against more. Some kinds of more shrink you, and some kinds grow you. Possessions pile up and need guarding. Wisdom, understanding and generosity pile up and set you free. And the surprise: giving looks like it should leave a person with less. Hillel says it leaves you with more peace. Then one more line: a person who has gained a good name has gained it for himself, but a person who has gained words of Torah has gained life in the world to come. A good name is precious, he seems to say, but it stays here. What you learn and give goes further. More isn't more. The question is always: more of what?

segments.voice: Picture walking slowly through your home, a closet, a drawer, a shelf, and find one thing you keep but don't need that someone else could use: a coat, a book, a pan. Notice the small tug of wanting to keep it. Then picture it in someone else's hands, being useful, and see if the tug loosens.
Marbeh de'agah. More possessions, more worry: the beat of Hillel's list, before it turns to more learning, more life, and more giving, more peace.
Your line: more giving, more peace. The whole list runs on one word, marbeh. Day two hundred fifty-six.

257.title: A good heart (Avot 2:9)
257.hook: Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students the best path; the answer that wins is a good heart
257.carry: everything else grows from the heart
257.tomorrow: repent a day before you die
257.howItsDone: This mishnah is studied as a portrait of character, and 'lev tov' is still an everyday Hebrew phrase for a kind, good-hearted person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel's chant: marbeh de'agah, more things, more worry. Your line was more giving, more peace.

A teacher gives his five students one assignment. No test, no essay. Just: go out and look at the world, then come back and tell me the one good path a person should hold on to. Five students, five answers. Then the teacher picks one, and explains why it wins. He's Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the student of Hillel, remembered as the sage who kept Jewish learning alive when Jerusalem fell to Rome. The winning answer is two Hebrew words: lev tov.
screen: `FIVE STUDENTS, ONE ASSIGNMENT.` → `YOCHANAN BEN ZAKKAI.` → `TWO WORDS WIN.`

segments.voice: Go out and see, he says, which is the good way a person should cling to. The five come back. Rabbi Eliezer says: a good eye, meaning a generous way of looking at people. Rabbi Joshua: a good friend. Rabbi Yose: a good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon: someone who sees what's coming, who thinks about the results of what they do. And Rabbi Elazar ben Arach: a good heart. Then the teacher speaks. I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arach, because his words include all of yours. Why? Generous seeing starts in the heart. A good friend and a good neighbor are what a good heart becomes when it lives near people. Even seeing what's coming depends on caring about who gets hurt. The heart is the root; the others are branches. In the Bible's Hebrew, the heart isn't just feelings. It's where a person thinks, decides and wants. So lev tov isn't only warmth. It's a whole inner life pointed toward the good. Then the Mishnah runs the same exercise backward. Which is the bad way a person should stay away from? A bad eye, a bad friend, a bad neighbor, someone who borrows and doesn't pay back, and, from Elazar ben Arach again, a bad heart. And again the teacher says: his words include all of yours.
screen: `GO OUT AND SEE THE GOOD WAY.` · `EYE, FRIEND, NEIGHBOR, FORESIGHT.` · `HIS WORDS INCLUDE ALL OF YOURS.` · `THE HEART IS THE ROOT.` · then, large: `LEV TOV: A GOOD HEART.`

segments.voice: Put a hand on your chest if that feels natural, and notice the heart going on quietly without you asking it to. Then walk the four branches: someone you could see more generously, a friend you could reach out to, a neighbor who needs something, one choice today whose results you could think through. Let each one come back to the heart.
Lev tov. A good heart: the answer Yochanan ben Zakkai chose, because it holds all the others inside it.
Your line: everything else grows from the heart. Five answers, one root. That's two hundred fifty-seven.

258.title: Repent a day before you die (Avot 2:10)
258.hook: Rabbi Eliezer: repent one day before your death, and no one knows the day, so every day
258.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats teshuvah, returning, as possible every day, not only on Yom Kippur, and the traditional bedtime prayers include a moment of forgiving others before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five students, five answers, and the one that held all the others. Your line was everything else grows from the heart. Today, one of those students speaks.

Rabbi Eliezer's students heard him say something that sounded impossible: repent one day before your death. So they asked the obvious question. How is anyone supposed to know which day that is? Eliezer was one of yesterday's five, the one his own teacher compared to a plastered cistern that never loses a drop. He had heard a great deal and lost none of it. And his answer takes a far-off day and sets it down right here, in this one.
screen: `AN IMPOSSIBLE INSTRUCTION.` → `WHICH DAY IS THAT?` → `A CISTERN THAT LOSES NOTHING.`

segments.voice: He said three things. Let your friend's honor be as dear to you as your own. Don't be quick to anger. And repent one day before your death. That last one is the riddle, and the Talmud records his answer to the students. Does anyone know the day he'll die? All the more reason to repent today, in case you die tomorrow. Then all your days will be spent in repentance. The word is teshuvah. It's usually translated repentance, but it really means return, or turning. You notice you've wandered off the path, and you turn back toward it. No groveling, no drama. Just a turn. Then a parable. A king invited his servants to a banquet, but didn't say when. The wise ones dressed in their best and waited by the palace door: a palace is never short of anything, so the feast could start any minute. The foolish ones went off to their work, saying there's no banquet without a lot of preparation first. Suddenly the king called them in. The wise walked in dressed and ready. The foolish came in dirty from work, and weren't allowed to sit at the table. The verse that goes with it is in Ecclesiastes, which in the JPS translation reads, "Let thy garments be always white." Not out of fear. Just ready. Eliezer's advice isn't a threat. It's a schedule. If today might be the day, then today is the day to turn.
screen: `THREE PIECES OF ADVICE.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE DAY.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `THE KING'S BANQUET.` · then, large: `LET THY GARMENTS BE ALWAYS WHITE.`

segments.voice: Look back over the day so far, slowly, from waking up until now, and notice one moment where you drifted from the person you mean to be: a sharp word, a shortcut, a kindness skipped. Don't argue with it or punish yourself; just name it, and picture one small step back in the right direction. If you pray, you can bring it to God.
Teshuvah. Return, a turning back: Rabbi Eliezer's riddle solved by turning today, since nobody knows the day of death.
Your line: repent today. Teshuvah is a turn, not a trial. Day two fifty-eight, done.

259.title: A good eye (Avot 2:11)
259.hook: an evil eye, the bad urge and hatred of people drive a person out of the world
259.howItsDone: In Jewish ethics, ayin tovah, a good eye, means generosity and gladness at others' good fortune, and it is often taught alongside the laws of giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teshuvah: Rabbi Eliezer said repent one day before you die, and nobody knows the day. Your line was repent today.

A friend posts a photo of her new house. You tap the heart. And somewhere under the heart, there's a small, sour feeling. Why her? She didn't even work that hard. You'd never say it out loud. But you felt it. Everybody has. Two days ago, Rabbi Eliezer's answer to the teacher's question was a good eye. Today another of those five students, Rabbi Joshua, describes the opposite. And he says it doesn't just spoil your mood. It drives you out of the world.
screen: `THE HEART UNDER THE PHOTO.` → `A SMALL, SOUR FEELING.` → `RABBI JOSHUA'S WARNING.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Joshua says three things drive a person out of the world: an evil eye, the bad urge, and hatred of people. The evil eye isn't what you might think. In the Mishnah, it isn't a curse or a spell. It's a way of looking: a stingy, begrudging eye, the eye that sees someone else's good fortune and wishes, a little, that they didn't have it. A good eye is the opposite: glad when others do well, and giving freely. Proverbs says the one with a bountiful eye is blessed, because he shares his bread with the poor. The Hebrew there is tov ayin, literally good of eye. Then the bad urge, the yetzer hara, the pull toward the selfish thing. And hatred of people, of anyone at all. Why would these drive you out of the world? Commentators give several answers. One is simple: they make you miserable, and wear your life down. Another is that they cut you off. If every friend's good news stings, you slowly stop being able to be with people. You end up alone in a crowd. The good eye opens the world back up: when you can be glad for others, their joy becomes a little bit yours. And that closes a week of Hillel and his heirs: you haven't been there, be a mensch, harm comes back, more isn't more, a good heart, repent today, and now, a good eye.
screen: `THREE THINGS DRIVE YOU OUT.` · `THE EVIL EYE: A BEGRUDGING LOOK.` · `TOV AYIN: GOOD OF EYE.` · `ALONE IN A CROWD, OR GLAD.` · then, large: `A GOOD EYE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose good news stung a little, a promotion, a trip, a new relationship, and don't pretend the sting isn't there. Then slowly picture them enjoying what they have, their face, their relief, and wish it for them sincerely, with no but at the end. If it's hard, start small, and try again.
Ayin tovah. A good eye, a generous way of seeing: glad when others do well, the opposite of the begrudging eye that drives a person out of the world.
Your line: glad when others do well. Tov ayin, good of eye. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: What's an evil eye in the Mishnah? Is it like a curse?
options: Not a curse. It's a begrudging way of seeing someone else's good fortune.
A tired, unfocused eye that keeps a person from noticing what's going on.
Looking at your own faults so much that you forget to notice others.
chat.meaning: In the Mishnah the evil eye is a stingy, begrudging way of looking. A good eye is glad when others do well, and gives freely.
